title: The boy at the door
hook: Parvati makes a son from earth; sets him to guard her bath
tomorrow: the boy says no to the next one at the door. who is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the first camp on a battlefield, with Krishna's line: you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Now the stories start, and the first one starts at a closed door.
screen: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: You know the sound. You're in the shower, or halfway through a hard phone call, and someone rattles the handle. Parvati knows it too. She lives with Shiva on Mount Kailash, and every guard at the door is one of his ganas, his attendants, loyal to him. Whenever Shiva wants in, they step aside. Nobody in that house is simply hers. So before her bath she takes the paste she rubbed on her skin, the dust of her own body, and shapes a boy. She breathes life into him. The first face he ever sees is his mother's. She hands him a staff. He has only just opened his eyes, and already he has a job. Guard this door. No one comes in.
screen: `SOMEONE RATTLES THE HANDLE.` → `NOBODY IN THE HOUSE IS HERS.` → `A BOY FROM THE DUST OF A BATH.` → `NO ONE COMES IN.`

segments.voice: That boy grows up to be Ganesha, the god you met on day one. This telling is the Shiva Purana's, a collection of stories about Shiva, and it isn't the only version; in it, her friends Jaya and Vijaya are the ones who say she needs a guard of her own. Here's the part people repeat later: the god of beginnings begins as the stuff you wash off in a bath. No thunder, no sky. Earth, shaped by a mother's hands. And look at why she makes him. Not loneliness. A door. In a house where every guard answers to someone else, she wants one person whose whole job is her space. The boy is brand new. He doesn't know who lives here, or who outranks whom. He knows one instruction, and he means it completely. Ganesha images often hang by front doors and shop entrances: he's honored as the keeper of thresholds, where outside becomes inside. Some things need a guard. A bath. A conversation you're not ready to have in front of everyone. The first quiet hour of a morning. And somewhere down the mountain, someone very large is walking home.
screen: `THE STUFF OF A BATH.` · `SHE NEEDS A DOOR, NOT COMPANY.` · `NEW, WITH ONE INSTRUCTION.` · `THE KEEPER OF THRESHOLDS.` · then, large: `SOME THINGS NEED A GUARD.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, you get to be the boy. Close your eyes and picture a door to a room that's only yours. When something knocks, a message, a worry, the replay of an argument, don't fight it: notice it, say not now, and let it wait outside. Then go back to standing at the door.
Ganas: Shiva's attendants, the guards of his house. Keep an eye on them. The boy made of earth is going to end up leading them.
Your line: some things need a guard. Parvati made hers out of earth. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 22 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO WALKS UP TO THAT DOOR?`

howItsDone: Some Hindu families keep an image of Ganesha by the front door or at the entrance of a shop, as the guardian of thresholds, and his birth story is often retold at Ganesh Chaturthi.

original.note: Sanskrit: lord (isha) of the ganas, the attendants. The boy at the door grows into their leader.
